name: FPGA-NFC
firmware_note: The Verilog is the entire product - there is no separate firmware/hardware split. It targets any FPGA (Altera Cyclone IV by default for the 81.36MHz PLL primitive; other vendors need a substitute clock IP).
price_note: No product exists to buy - $20 is a rough BOM estimate for the NFC_BreakoutBoard (AD7276B ADC, FDV301N MOSFET, coil, passives) via the linked OSHWHub gerbers, and does not include the FPGA dev board itself (any board with a spare clock, 4 GPIO and a UART bridge works; a cheap Cyclone IV board runs $15-40 more).
skill_note: You are writing and debugging the ISO14443A PHY and MAC layers yourself in Verilog, then soldering an analogue front end and tuning a 4-turn antenna coil by hand. This is an RF and digital-logic project, not a 'buy and flash' tool.
build_note: Fabricate the NFC_BreakoutBoard PCB from the provided gerbers, hand-solder the AD7276B ADC and analogue front end, wire it to any FPGA dev board's GPIO (ADC_SCK runs at up to 40.68MHz, so the README explicitly warns against Dupont jumper wires), then synthesize and load the Verilog.
summary: A from-scratch ISO14443A card reader built entirely in FPGA logic and a handful of discrete parts (a 3Msps AD7276B ADC, an FDV301N MOSFET, a diode envelope detector and a 4-turn coil) instead of a dedicated NFC chip like the PN532 or ST25R3916. It talks to a host PC over a plain 9600-baud serial line and has been demonstrated reading MIFARE Classic (M1) cards. It's a teaching/hobby project by a single developer, not a product.
honest_take: This does exactly one useful thing that a $9 PN532 breakout doesn't: it proves the NFC PHY layer isn't magic - carrier generation, ASK demodulation via envelope detection, and the ISO14443A frame format are all implemented in visible, readable Verilog. But as a tool it is strictly worse than a PN532 or Proxmark3 for any practical RFID work: no write support beyond the protocol layer, no anti-collision beyond basic REQA/ANTICOLL, no MIFARE Classic crypto attacks, and a carrier that auto-shuts-off after 1.2 seconds of serial inactivity. Buy this only if the point is learning FPGA-based RF signal processing; buy a PN532 if the point is reading cards.
best_for: Learning how ISO14443A's ASK envelope detection and framing actually work at the signal level
FPGA/Verilog practice with a real RF front end
Demonstrating that dedicated NFC silicon isn't required for basic 13.56MHz reading
not_for: Anyone who just wants to read/clone/emulate NFC cards - buy a PN532 or Proxmark3 instead
MIFARE Classic key-recovery attacks (nested/darkside/hardnested) - not implemented
Any use requiring tag emulation - this project only implements the PCD (reader) role

hardware.mcu_primary_note: No MCU. Protocol logic, DSP, and UART framing all run as Verilog RTL inside the FPGA fabric (any FPGA large enough for a small UART+DSP design; author used an Altera Cyclone IV).

radios.note: 3Msps 12-bit SPI ADC, used to sample the 847.5kHz subcarrier envelope from the PICC-to-PCD response, not the 13.56MHz carrier directly.

hardware.battery_note: None. Powered from the FPGA board's USB/external supply plus a separate 7-9V rail for the antenna drive circuit (J1 on the breakout board).
hardware.storage: None - all logic is synthesized into FPGA fabric, no persistent storage
connectivity: UART (via the FPGA board's own USB-UART bridge, e.g. FT232/CP2102/CH340)
hardware.gpio: 4 FPGA GPIO pins used: ADC_CSN, ADC_SCLK, ADC_SDATA, CARRIER_OUT, at 3.3V or 2.5V logic
notable_physical: 4-turn hand-wound antenna coil on the breakout PCB
Separate 7-9V supply input for the carrier drive MOSFET
Onboard status LEDs for PLL lock, carrier-on, and RX-complete

hf_1356_read.note: Full ISO14443A PHY/MAC in Verilog; demonstrated reading MIFARE Classic (M1) cards including door-control cards and blank white cards.

hf_1356_write.note: README states the protocol layer supports send/receive framing, but no ready-made write/format application is provided - you'd write the M1 write commands yourself over serial.

hf_1356_emulate.note: Only implements the PCD (reader) role, not PICC (card) emulation.

mifare_classic_attacks.note: No key-recovery or crypto attacks implemented - this is a bare reader, not a Proxmark-style attack tool.

iso15693.note: README says the analogue hardware supports ISO15693, but the Verilog protocol layer for it was never written ('I haven't write its protocol in FPGA').

scriptable.note: Plain-text hex-over-serial protocol at 9600 baud, one command/response per line - trivial to script from any language.

standalone_untethered.note: Requires a host PC sending serial commands; the FPGA auto-cuts the carrier 1.2s after the last command with nothing to reissue it.

legal.notes: A bare-metal 13.56MHz reader you build and program yourself. Owning and reading cards you're authorized to read (your own access cards, your own tags) is not restricted in most jurisdictions. Reading or cloning someone else's access credentials without authorization is a separate legal question wherever you are - check local law before pointing it at a card that isn't yours.

sources.what: full README: block diagram, part numbers (AD7276B, FDV301N, 1N4148), serial protocol, M1 card interaction log
OSHWHub page hosting the NFC_BreakoutBoard PCB design referenced from the README

research_gaps: No documented TX field strength or read range in mm/cm - author reports successful reads but not a measured distance.
No independent teardown or third-party reproduction found; all technical claims trace back to the single author's own README.

name: RFID HF Repeater Large
price_note: $20.00 at Hacker Warehouse (SKU MWG-V3L). No listed price history from other sellers.
skill_note: It's a passive card-sized resonator - place it between the obstruction and the reader. No configuration, no firmware, no electronics knowledge needed.
build_note: Fully passive, ready to use out of the box - nothing to assemble or program.
summary: A passive, unpowered 13.56MHz resonant coil in a 3x3 inch card, sold to relay a reader's HF field through an obstruction (a wallet, a bag, a thin door panel) and recover a few millimeters of lost read range. Hacker Warehouse's own listing quotes an example gain of 5-9mm of extra read distance - it is a physics accessory for RFID work, not an active device.
honest_take: This is a tuned LC resonator, not an amplifier - it has no battery and no active gain stage, so it cannot make a card readable from meters away or defeat a Faraday-shielded wallet; it only recovers the few millimeters an obstruction otherwise costs you, and how much depends entirely on how well its resonant frequency and coupling geometry happen to match your reader and card. For genuine long-range HF field manipulation (the kind used in real relay/ghost-and-leech attacks) you want an active repeater built from two coupled reader/emulator stages with real amplification, not a passive card like this one.
best_for: Recovering a few mm of NFC/RFID read range lost to a phone case, wallet or thin door panel
Physical pentest kits where a slightly thicker badge holder is defeating quick taps
not_for: Long-range relay attacks (meters, not millimeters) - needs an active two-stage repeater, not a passive card
Defeating RFID-blocking (Faraday) wallets or sleeves - a passive resonator cannot punch through shielding

hardware.mcu_primary_note: None. Fully passive resonant LC circuit - no active components.

radios.note: Passive printed/etched coil tuned to 13.56MHz, no dedicated IC - just a resonant loop antenna and matching network.

hardware.battery_note: None - fully passive, no power source of any kind.
hardware.dimensions_mm: 76 x 76 x 5 (3 x 3 x 0.2 in per vendor listing)
notable_physical: Card form factor, placed flat between reader and obstruction

hf_1356_read.note: Not a reader itself - a passive field relay placed between an existing reader and a card to recoup lost coupling distance.

legal.notes: A passive antenna accessory with no transmitter of its own - it does not generate RF energy, only relays an existing reader's field, so it isn't a separate radio device under most regulatory schemes. Using it to improve your own card's read reliability is unremarkable; using it covertly to improve unauthorized access to a card reader you don't own is the same legal territory as any other unauthorized-access tool in your jurisdiction.

sources.what: product listing: price, dimensions, weight, SKU, example 5-9mm range gain, vendor Midwest Gadgets

research_gaps: No schematic or coil design published - resonant frequency tuning and Q factor are unverifiable claims from the retail listing alone.
Could not find Midwest Gadgets' own product page independent of the Hacker Warehouse reseller listing.

name: Mellon
firmware_note: A Python proof-of-concept toolkit, not firmware for a fixed device - it runs on a laptop and drives generic USB-to-RS485 adapters.
price_note: The code is free; $15 is a rough estimate for one generic USB-to-RS485 adapter. A full active man-in-the-middle setup needs three adapters per the README (roughly $30-45 total) plus a breadboard, not counting the laptop you run the Python on.
skill_note: You need to understand OSDP wiring (RS485 A/B, controller vs. reader roles), physically tap or insert into the wiring between a door controller and a reader, and interpret raw protocol captures - this is not a point-and-click tool.
build_note: No enclosure or kit - wire up to three USB-to-RS485 adapters on a breadboard per Bishop Fox's own setup and run the Python scripts (attack_osdp.py) against the physical RS485 bus, or against the included vulnserver.py to practice without hardware.
summary: Bishop Fox's reference proof-of-concept toolkit for attacking OSDP (Open Supervised Device Protocol), the RS485 protocol that connects most modern access-control card readers to their door controllers. It implements the five attacks from their 2023 Black Hat/DEF CON research 'Badge of Shame': passive eavesdropping of unencrypted card numbers, forcing an encryption downgrade, extracting the shared key during install mode, capturing keys sent during a key-rotation, and brute-forcing weak/default keys. It's a research tool released alongside the talk, not a commercial product.
honest_take: Mellon is the reference implementation behind real, disclosed OSDP weaknesses - not marketing. The catch is that most of its attacks (downgrade, install-mode key extraction, weak-key brute force) require physical access to the RS485 wire between reader and controller, which usually means opening a reader or getting inside a wiring closet; this is a wired-access-control research tool, not a wireless card-cloning tool like a Proxmark or Flipper. The single most common misconception is treating this as a plug-and-play badge cloner - it attacks the wire, not the card, and it needs real RS485 hardware and OSDP protocol knowledge to use at all.
best_for: Physical penetration testers validating whether a client's OSDP install actually uses Secure Channel encryption
Learning OSDP's actual wire-level weaknesses from the tool that demonstrated them
Practicing against the bundled vulnserver.py without needing real access-control hardware
not_for: Wireless/contactless card cloning - this attacks the RS485 wire between reader and controller, not the card-to-reader RF link
Anyone without RS485/OSDP wiring knowledge or physical access to the reader-controller cable

hardware.mcu_primary_note: None built-in. Mellon is software; it depends on off-the-shelf USB-to-RS485 adapters (the README names generic units, not a specific chipset) to reach the physical bus.
hardware.battery_note: None - runs on a laptop; the RS485 adapters are USB-bus powered.
notable_physical: No dedicated hardware - a breadboard of up to three generic USB-RS485 adapters wired to the OSDP bus for full MITM

uart.note: Speaks RS485/OSDP directly over the wire via USB-to-RS485 adapters - not UART in the microcontroller-debug sense, but the same serial family.

scriptable.note: Pure Python; attack_osdp.py implements the attacks and vulnserver.py provides an intentionally-vulnerable OSDP controller for offline testing.

legal.notes: The code itself is a legal research tool, published openly by a security firm alongside a conference talk. Actually wiring into an OSDP bus you don't own or control - to eavesdrop on card numbers, downgrade encryption, or extract keys from someone else's access-control system - is unauthorized access to a security system in most jurisdictions, independent of how the eavesdropping is technically done. Only use it against systems you own or have written authorization to test.

sources.what: README: attack list, USB-RS485 adapter count for full MITM, vulnserver.py test harness, license
Bishop Fox 'Badge of Shame' research writeup naming the five OSDP attacks Mellon implements
DEF CON 31 slide deck detailing the attacks and Mellon's role as the PoC tool

research_gaps: No specific USB-to-RS485 adapter chipset (e.g. FTDI vs CH340) is named as required or recommended in the README.

name: RFIDetector
price_note: No retail listing exists anywhere - $15 is an unverified low estimate for a credit-card-sized PCB with two coils, a handful of Schottky diodes and LEDs. Treat this figure as a guess, not a sourced price.
skill_note: Small SMD passive/diode design - buildable by anyone comfortable hand-soldering fine-pitch parts, but you're fabricating the PCB yourself from KiCad files with no vendor to buy it assembled.
build_note: CERN-OHL-S licensed KiCad hardware (schematic + PCB, revision history rev0.1 through rev0.22) with no assembled option - order the boards yourself and hand-solder the parts.
summary: A small open-hardware PCB (CERN-OHL-S licensed) that indicates whether it is sitting in an active LF (125kHz) or HF (13.56MHz) RFID reader field. Inspection of the schematic shows it is a purely passive/analogue design - two tuned coils, nine 1N5819WS Schottky diodes for envelope detection on each band, and three status LEDs, with solder-jumper pads to select modes - not a microcontroller-based device.
honest_take: This is a passive field-presence indicator, not a reader or a security scanner: it tells you 'something nearby is generating an LF or HF field,' not what protocol, what data, or whose reader it is. It has no microcontroller, no logging, and no way to distinguish a legitimate access-control reader from a skimmer or from your own Flipper Zero sitting in your pocket. With 3 GitHub stars and a single contributor it is effectively a personal project shared as open hardware, not a maintained product - expect to debug your own PCB order.
best_for: Quickly confirming a suspected reader/skimmer is actually emitting an LF or HF field before further investigation
Learning passive envelope-detection RFID sensing circuit design from real KiCad source
not_for: Identifying what protocol or data a reader is using - it only distinguishes LF vs HF presence
Any kind of card reading, cloning, or logging - it has no data-capture capability at all

hardware.mcu_primary_note: None. Schematic inspection (rev0.22) shows a purely discrete/analogue circuit: two tuned coils, nine 1N5819WS Schottky diodes for envelope detection, ~10uF caps, and solder-jumper mode-select pads - no microcontroller anywhere on the board.

radios.note: Passive tuned coil + diode envelope detector, LED-only indication, no data decode.
Passive tuned coil + diode envelope detector, LED-only indication, no data decode.

hardware.battery_note: Not documented; no battery holder visible in the schematic bill of materials found. Likely coin-cell or field-powered - unconfirmed.
sensors: LF/HF field-presence (via envelope-detector diodes, LED indication only)
notable_physical: Three status LEDs
Solder-jumper pads for mode selection
Two separate tuned antenna coils (LF and HF) on one PCB

lf_125khz_read.note: Detects field presence only via diode envelope detection and an LED - does not decode or display tag data.

hf_1356_read.note: Same - field-presence indication only, no data decode.

legal.notes: A passive receive-only indicator with no transmitter and no data capture. Owning or building one raises no meaningful legal concern in most jurisdictions; it does not read, store, or transmit any card data.

sources.what: repo README (purpose statement, CERN-OHL-S-2.0 license) and file tree (hardware/rev0.1-0.22, simulation, tuner)
KiCad schematic (rev0.22) inspected directly: confirms 1N5819WS diode envelope detectors, LEDs, and absence of any MCU

research_gaps: No documented detection range or sensitivity threshold.
No confirmed real-world sale price - the $15 figure is an unverified estimate, not a vendor quote.
Could not determine intended power source (battery type, if any) from available files.

name: simple_rfid
firmware_note: Arduino sketch is the entire firmware; no alternate builds exist.
price_note: Rough BOM estimate: an Arduino Nano clone (~$3-5) plus an RDM6300 125kHz reader module (~$3-5). PCB manufacturing through the linked PCBWay project adds a few dollars per board in small quantities on top of that.
skill_note: Off-the-shelf Arduino Nano + RDM6300 module wired per the schematic and flashed with the provided sketch - straightforward for anyone who has done basic Arduino projects, no RF design of your own required.
build_note: Schematic and PCB layout provided (with a PCBWay fabrication link); solder the Nano and RDM6300 module to the board and flash the Arduino sketch from the firmware folder.
summary: A DIY 125kHz LF RFID reader/cloner/emulator built from an Arduino Nano and an off-the-shelf RDM6300 reader module, with open schematic, PCB layout and firmware. It targets the same basic EM4100/T5577-class tags as any generic 125kHz copier - the RDM6300 module does the actual RF demodulation, the Arduino handles UID capture, storage and re-transmission.
honest_take: The RDM6300 module underneath this is the same cheap part found in countless $5-10 'generic 125kHz RFID copier' kits already on the market and already in this database - this project's value is that it's open source and buildable from raw parts rather than bought as a sealed grey-market unit, not that it does anything those kits don't. It only covers 125kHz LF (EM4100/T5577-class) tags - it has no HF/13.56MHz capability at all, so it can't touch MIFARE or any modern access card.
best_for: Learning how a 125kHz reader/cloner actually works by building one from an Arduino and a commodity reader module
Cheap DIY alternative to a sealed generic 125kHz copier for basic EM4100/T5577 cloning
not_for: Any 13.56MHz/HF card (MIFARE, DESFire, NFC phones) - this is LF-only
Rolling-code or encrypted credentials - RDM6300-based readers only handle plain fixed-ID LF tags

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Standard Arduino Nano board handling UID storage and control logic.

radios.note: Off-the-shelf 125kHz reader module (EM4100-class); handles RF demodulation and outputs UID over UART to the Arduino.

hardware.battery_note: Not specified - USB or external 5V supply typical for this class of Arduino+RDM6300 build.
hardware.storage: Arduino onboard EEPROM/flash for storing captured UIDs (typical for this class of project; not explicitly detailed in available README excerpt)
hardware.gpio: Arduino Nano digital/analog pins, mostly consumed by the RDM6300 UART link
notable_physical: RDM6300 module with its own LF antenna coil
PCB and schematic files, PCBWay fabrication link

lf_125khz_read.note: Via the RDM6300 module; reads standard EM4100-class 125kHz tags.

lf_125khz_write.note: Vendor/README describes it as a 'cloner' implying write-capable target tags (e.g. T5577), but the specific write mechanism wasn't independently confirmed from available source excerpts.

lf_125khz_emulate.note: README describes 'emulator' functionality; exact implementation (which chip drives the emulated field) not confirmed from available excerpts.

hf_1356_read.note: No HF hardware present - RDM6300 is LF-only, and no 13.56MHz front end is included in this design.

legal.notes: A DIY LF RFID reader/cloner is legal to own and build in most jurisdictions - it's functionally similar to any generic 125kHz copier already sold openly. Using it to read or clone an access card you don't own or aren't authorized to duplicate is a separate matter, governed by local unauthorized-access and fraud law rather than by anything specific to the hardware.

name: HiLetgo PN532 NFC RFID Module Kit
price_note: $8.99 is a representative Amazon marketplace price for a PN532 breakout of this class; HiLetgo and near-identical clone boards from other brands (Elechouse, generic) commonly sell in the $8-15 range depending on antenna size and included accessories.
skill_note: A bare breakout board - you wire it to a microcontroller or SBC over I2C/SPI/UART and run libnfc or a vendor SDK yourself; no standalone app.
build_note: No soldering typically required beyond header pins (often pre-soldered); wire to a Raspberry Pi, Arduino or similar host and install libnfc or an equivalent driver.
summary: A breakout board for NXP's PN532, the NFC controller chip found in the overwhelming majority of phones and consumer NFC readers, exposing I2C, SPI and UART (HSU) interfaces. It reads and writes NFC Type 1-4 tags and MIFARE Classic/Ultralight, and can do ISO18092 peer-to-peer and (with the right firmware/library support) basic card emulation - it is the standard low-cost building block behind countless libnfc, Arduino and Raspberry Pi RFID projects.
honest_take: This is genuinely the same silicon inside a large share of commercial NFC readers, not a toy chip - the PN532's read/write/P2P/emulation feature set is real. What you're paying $9 for is a breakout with a stripline antenna and level shifting, not a finished tool: there's no screen, no standalone operation, no MIFARE Classic key-cracking, and getting reliable I2C/SPI communication out of the cheaper clone boards (address conflicts, flaky IRQ handling) is a known headache in the libnfc community. If you want a point-and-use device rather than a module to wire up yourself, a Flipper Zero or ACR122U is the better buy; if you're building your own project on a Pi or microcontroller, this is the standard part to reach for.
best_for: DIY NFC projects on Arduino/Raspberry Pi/ESP32 via libnfc or vendor libraries
Reading/writing NDEF, MIFARE Classic/Ultralight tags on a budget
Peer-to-peer NFC experiments (ISO18092)
not_for: Standalone use without a host microcontroller/SBC and your own code
MIFARE Classic key-recovery attacks - the PN532 alone doesn't implement nested/darkside/hardnested attacks; you'd need to build that on top in software
Reliable production use without budgeting time for clone-board I2C/antenna quality issues

hardware.mcu_primary_note: None onboard beyond the PN532 itself, which contains its own internal 80C51 microcontroller core (per NXP's PN532 datasheet) but is not separately user-programmable on these breakouts.

radios.note: NXP's NFC controller: ISO14443A (MIFARE Classic/Ultralight), ISO14443B, FeliCa, and ISO18092 peer-to-peer, 13.56MHz, reader/writer and limited card-emulation modes depending on firmware/library support.

hardware.battery_note: None - powered from the host (3.3-5V depending on board variant).
hardware.gpio: Standard 0.1in header pins for interface selection jumpers and IRQ/RSTPDN lines
notable_physical: Onboard tuned stripline PCB antenna
Interface-select jumpers/switch for I2C/SPI/UART mode

hf_1356_read.note: Via PN532 hardware, reads ISO14443A/MIFARE and FeliCa cards; requires host code (libnfc, Adafruit PN532 library, etc.).

hf_1356_write.note: Standard PN532 write support for MIFARE Classic/Ultralight and NDEF-formatted tags via libnfc/vendor libraries.

hf_1356_emulate.note: PN532 supports card-emulation mode in hardware, but reliable emulation depends heavily on host library/firmware support - flaky on many clone boards per widespread community reports.

nfc_type4_ndef.note: NDEF read/write supported via libnfc/Adafruit-style libraries.

Reading or duplicating access credentials or payment cards you don't own or lack authorization for is the legal risk, and depends on local unauthorized-access and fraud law, not on the hardware itself.

representative marketplace listing/pricing for HiLetgo-branded PN532 V3 kit

name: MACOBOX
price_note: Lab401 lists it at $11,000 USD (approx. EUR2,700-listed on some regional pages, likely a currency-display glitch or a stripped-down SKU; the fuller EUR9,700 price with the full 12-month support bundle is closer to the USD figure and is treated as the defensible number here).
skill_note: Built for professional hardware pentest engagements - rapid multi-interface firmware extraction (UART/SPI/JTAG/I2C/SWD) assumes you already know how to identify and wire test points on unknown PCBs.
build_note: Ships as a complete kit: the MACOBOX unit itself plus a Sensepeek PCBite probe kit, an AllSocket eMMC reader, a multimeter, SOP flash sockets, SPI clips, connectors, a precision screwdriver set, jumper kit and portable carrying plate.
summary: A self-contained hardware-pentest lab-in-a-box from Mindstorm Security: a Cortex-A53-based Linux appliance (1.5GHz, 4GB RAM, 256GB storage, Wi-Fi/BLE/LAN/4 USB) bundled with a full physical toolkit (PCBite probes, eMMC reader, SOP flash sockets, SPI clips) for connecting to and dumping firmware from UART, SPI, JTAG, I2C and SWD interfaces on unknown target boards, plus cloud-based firmware vulnerability analysis and FCC-ID-driven project generation. The $11k price includes 12 months of vendor support and three free replacement/addon boards per year.
honest_take: This is priced and positioned as a subscription service wrapped around hardware, not a one-time tool purchase - the headline price buys you a year of engineering support, hardware replacement and a cloud analysis pipeline, and it's unclear what the device is worth once that year lapses without renewing. Every interface it exposes (UART, SPI, JTAG, I2C, SWD) is also covered by tools costing a tiny fraction of $11k - a Tigard, Bus Pirate 5, or JTAGulator plus a laptop covers the same protocols for well under $200 combined, with an enormously larger open community behind them. The case for MACOBOX is workflow speed and vendor support in a professional engagement where billable hours matter more than hardware cost, not raw capability you can't get elsewhere.
best_for: Professional hardware pentest teams who bill by the hour and want a single supported kit instead of assembling and maintaining a toolbox of point tools
Engagements needing fast FCC-ID-driven target identification and a managed cloud vulnerability pipeline
not_for: Hobbyists or anyone price-sensitive - a Tigard/Bus Pirate/JTAGulator combination covers the same protocols for a fraction of the cost
Anyone who doesn't want an ongoing vendor support relationship - the price bundles 12 months of subscription-style service

Precision screwdriver and jumper kit

Dumping firmware from a device you don't own or lack authorization to test is the same legal issue it would be with any debug tool.

name: ChipSHOVER
price_note: $10,000 direct from NewAE, quoted with a 2-week lead time as of the vendor's own page.
skill_note: A precision robotics platform for automated EM fault-injection mapping across a die surface - assumes you already understand fault injection and side-channel methodology; the ChipSHOVER only automates the physical positioning.
build_note: Ships assembled as a complete XYZ stage; controlled via onboard LCD for manual jogging or a Python API for scripted scans.
summary: A motorized 3-axis XYZ positioning stage from NewAE (45cm square base, 5cm travel per axis, sub-200nm precision, ~4um repeatability) built to automate scanning an EM fault-injection probe or side-channel sensor across a chip's surface - something normally done by hand with a manual micromanipulator. It includes a direct mounting adapter for NewAE's own ChipSHOUTER EM fault-injection tool, and is controlled either from its onboard LCD or scripted over USB via Python.
honest_take: Despite the name similarity to the ChipSHOUTER, this is a completely different product - the ChipSHOUTER is the EM pulse generator itself, the ChipSHOVER is the robot arm that moves it (or any other probe) around a chip automatically. It does not inject faults or do side-channel capture on its own; you still need a ChipSHOUTER, an EM probe, or other sensing hardware to actually do the work, this just automates the tedious manual XY-scanning that fault-injection research otherwise requires. At $10k it's a pure research-lab-tier automation accessory - worthwhile only if you're already doing enough EMFI scanning by hand that a robotic stage pays for itself in time saved.
best_for: Automating EM fault-injection surface scans across a die that would otherwise require hours of manual micromanipulator repositioning
Research labs running repeatable, scripted EMFI or side-channel sweeps
not_for: Anyone without a ChipSHOUTER or other EM/side-channel probe already - the ChipSHOVER only positions a probe, it doesn't include one
One-off fault injection on a single known location - a manual micromanipulator is far cheaper for that

name: AutoProber
firmware_note: Python control package + Flask web dashboard is the entire software stack; no alternate builds exist.
price_note: $700 is a rough estimate for the core reference build (a SainSmart Genmitsu 3018-PROVer V2 CNC at roughly $250-350, a USB microscope at $30-80, 3D-printed toolhead parts, and probing hardware) - it explicitly excludes the Siglent SDS1104X-E oscilloscope used for the safety cutoff, which alone runs well over $1,000. Total realistic cost with the scope is closer to $2,000+.
skill_note: Integrates a GRBL CNC, a networked oscilloscope over SCPI, computer-vision pad detection and pogo-probe measurement into one automated stack - assumes you can already do manual PCB probing and are comfortable wiring/calibrating CNC motion control and scope triggering.
build_note: No kit is sold - you source a GRBL-compatible CNC (Genmitsu 3018-PROVer V2 in the reference build), a USB microscope, a LAN-connected Siglent SDS1104X-E oscilloscope, 3D-print the custom toolhead from provided CAD files, and run the Python/Flask control stack yourself.
summary: An open (source-available, noncommercial license) automation stack that turns a hobby CNC router, a USB microscope and a networked oscilloscope into a semi-autonomous PCB-probing rig: it maps a board via computer vision, identifies candidate pads/pins, lets an operator review targets through a web dashboard, then drives a 3D-printed pogo-probe toolhead to take operator-approved measurements with a scope-monitored safety cutoff that halts motion if voltage thresholds are exceeded.
honest_take: This replicates, on hobbyist CNC hardware, a category of automated flying-probe testing that is normally only found in expensive closed commercial lab equipment - genuinely notable. But 'AI agents independently perform PCB analysis' (the project's own framing) still means computer-vision pad detection feeding into an operator review step before any probe moves, not unsupervised autonomous probing of a live board; the safety cutoff over SCPI is the load-bearing part; nothing here replaces careful manual verification of what a probe is about to touch. It's also only 2 commits deep despite 330 stars, so this is a very early-stage project - budget for debugging the integration yourself, not a turnkey system.
best_for: Hardware hackers repeatedly probing similar/repetitive boards who want to automate the tedious repositioning of manual probing
Anyone already owning a GRBL CNC and a SCPI-capable oscilloscope who wants to add camera-guided, safety-monitored probing on top

name: PhyWhisperer-USB (CW610)
price_note: $360 direct from NewAE; Crowd Supply lists the same board at $365.
skill_note: An in-line USB protocol monitor/trigger for timing side-channel and fault-injection captures against USB targets - assumes familiarity with USB 2.0 protocol framing and with ChipWhisperer-style capture workflows.
build_note: Ships assembled; sits in-line on the USB cable between host and target, controlled from Python.
summary: A Xilinx Spartan-7S15-based in-line USB 2.0 Low/Full/High-Speed monitor and pattern trigger. It buffers 8,192 bytes of captured USB traffic in FPGA block RAM, fires a cycle-accurate trigger when 1-64 bytes of masked pattern match, includes a power shunt for correlating captures with power draw on an external scope, and feeds synchronized clock/trigger signals to ChipWhisperer capture hardware for USB-target power analysis and fault injection.
honest_take: This is a precision timing/triggering instrument, not a USB sniffer for casual protocol analysis - Wireshark with a USB capture driver, or a cheap USB protocol analyzer, does general-purpose USB traffic inspection far more conveniently. PhyWhisperer-USB earns its keep specifically for side-channel and fault-injection work against USB-connected targets, where you need a trigger that fires on exact protocol bytes with cycle-accurate timing synced to a ChipWhisperer - a niche need, but one nothing else in this price range addresses.

Labs already running ChipWhisperer capture hardware against USB-connected targets
not_for: General-purpose USB protocol sniffing/debugging - a standard USB analyzer or Wireshark capture is more convenient for that
Anyone without ChipWhisperer capture hardware to synchronize it with - its main value is the sync clock/trigger feed

name: NewAE Probe Set with Power Supply
skill_note: Passive sensing accessories for power/EM side-channel analysis - useful only if you already have a capture instrument (oscilloscope or ChipWhisperer) and know how to use differential/H-field probes for SCA.
build_note: Ships ready to use: isolated power module, three 6-pin probe cables, micro-USB cable and USB power adapter included alongside the three probes.
summary: An isolated USB-powered supply (5V USB in, delivering 3.3V for an LNA and +/-7.8V for a differential probe, with up to 50V isolation to prevent ground-loop contamination) sold together with three sensing probes: a differential probe for power-consumption analysis, an LNA probe and an H-field probe for electromagnetic side-channel measurement. It's a sensing accessory, not a capture instrument - you still need an oscilloscope or ChipWhisperer to record what the probes pick up.
honest_take: This is instrumentation, not an attack tool by itself - the differential and H-field probes measure power draw and EM emissions, which only becomes a side-channel attack once fed into capture and analysis software (ChipWhisperer or your own scope + DPA/CPA toolchain) and correlated against known plaintext/ciphertext. The isolated power supply is the unglamorous but important part: without galvanic isolation, ground loops between your target and your scope can swamp exactly the small signals these probes are trying to measure.

Safely isolating target power from measurement equipment to avoid ground-loop noise
not_for: Anyone without a capture instrument (scope/ChipWhisperer) already - these probes only sense, they don't record or analyze
Beginners to side-channel analysis - there's no guided workflow here, just raw sensing hardware

name: CW308 UFO Board
firmware_note: The UFO board itself carries no firmware; the repo hosts the target daughtercard designs (STM32F3, XMEGA, etc.) that plug into it.
price_note: $325 direct from NewAE; currently listed out of stock.
skill_note: The standard target platform for ChipWhisperer-based power analysis and glitching - assumes you already have a ChipWhisperer capture board and understand the basic DPA/CPA/glitching workflow; the UFO board itself is just the standardized victim-board plumbing.
build_note: Ships assembled with STM32F3 and XMEGA example target daughtercards plus blank prototyping PCBs for building your own targets; swap in other 8-bit, 32-bit or FPGA daughtercards as needed.
summary: NewAE's standard baseboard for building ChipWhisperer side-channel and glitching target ('victim') boards. It supplies clean, filtered power at 1.2V/1.8V/2.5V/3.3V and an adjustable 1.25-3.5V rail, a crystal-socket oscillator, an onboard LC low-pass filter for accurate shunt-based power measurement, and diode-protected I/O for voltage glitch injection - all shared infrastructure so a target daughtercard only needs to carry the chip under test.
honest_take: This is the unglamorous infrastructure board that makes ChipWhisperer side-channel work reproducible across different target chips - it does nothing attack-related by itself, it just standardizes power filtering, clocking and glitch-injection wiring so daughtercards (STM32F3, XMEGA, FPGA targets) can be swapped without re-engineering the measurement setup each time. It's the right board to own once you're doing serious ChipWhisperer work across multiple target chip families; if you only ever plan to attack one specific chip, a purpose-built single-target board is cheaper.
best_for: Standardized ChipWhisperer power-analysis and glitching setups across multiple target chip families
Building custom target daughtercards using the provided blank prototyping PCBs
not_for: Attacking a single specific chip long-term - a dedicated single-target board avoids paying for swappable-daughtercard infrastructure you won't use
